title: Scones
subtitle: Fluffy British cream tea scones
excerpt: Light, well-risen scones baked until golden, served warm with clotted cream and strawberry jam. The cornerstone of the British cream tea.

recipe.sourceNotes: Scones are central to the British cream tea tradition. They appear in Scottish and English cookbooks from the early 19th century and became associated with afternoon tea as that meal became fashionable among the Victorian middle classes. The cream tea itself is particularly associated with Devon and Cornwall, where the rival traditions of cream-first versus jam-first remain a matter of genuine regional pride: the Cornish spread jam first then cream, the Devonians cream first then jam. The scone itself should be light, well-risen, and just barely sweet, designed to carry the toppings rather than to be interesting on its own. The key to good scones is minimal handling: overworking the dough develops gluten and makes the scones tough. Handle them as little as possible.

recipeTools.notes: A flat baking tray, lightly floured.

content.text: The two rules for good scones: use cold butter and do not overwork the dough. Rub the butter in quickly and lightly with cold fingertips, or use a food processor for a few quick pulses. As soon as the dough comes together, stop. Pat it out rather than roll it: rolling puts more pressure on the dough and compresses it. Cut straight down with the cutter rather than twisting, or the scones will rise unevenly.

items.preparation: juice only, to sour the milk

content.text: Heat the oven to 220 C / fan 200 C / gas 7. Stir the lemon juice into the cold milk and set aside for 5 minutes. Sift the flour and salt into a bowl. Rub in the cold butter quickly with your fingertips until the mixture resembles fine breadcrumbs. Stir in the sugar.

Make a well in the centre and pour in the milk. Mix with a round-bladed knife until just combined. The dough will be slightly sticky. Turn onto a lightly floured surface and pat out, handling as little as possible, to about 2.5 cm thick.

Cut out rounds with a 6 cm plain cutter, pressing straight down without twisting. Place on a floured tray. Brush the tops with beaten egg. Bake for 12 to 15 minutes until well risen and golden. Serve warm.
